title: Roots, plexus and nerves: the map problem
description: Three overlapping maps cover every limb; choosing the one muscle or reflex that tells them apart is the art.
why: Three overlapping maps cover every limb; the art is choosing the muscle or reflex that tells root, plexus and nerve apart.
objectives: Distinguish a dermatome, a myotome and a nerve territory, and explain why one root lesion may numb very little.
Apply the two rules: every muscle a nerve supplies below the lesion must be weak; test a muscle with the same root but a different nerve.
Tell a common peroneal neuropathy from an L5 radiculopathy at the bedside.
Localize a brachial plexus birth injury to the roots or the trunks using the root-level branches.
Use the tendon reflexes as root markers, and recognize the cord's lost-here, brisk-below pattern.

sections.title: Three maps laid over one limb
sections.content:
Every limb is covered by three maps at once, and they do not agree. The **dermatome** is the skin a single dorsal root supplies. The **myotome** is the set of muscles a single ventral root supplies. The **nerve territory** is what one named peripheral nerve supplies after the plexus has shuffled the roots together. Brazis puts it plainly: localizing a root lesion requires precise knowledge of each myotome and dermatome, and separating it from a plexus or nerve lesion depends on the segmental character of the signs (Brazis 2011, p. 89).

**Why one root may numb so little**

Adjacent roots overlap generously on the skin. Brazis notes that cutting a single dorsal root produces little or no sensory loss, so a normal sensory exam does not exclude a root lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 89). Root lesions announce themselves more often with pain: sharp, electric, radiating along the root's territory and made worse by coughing, straining or sneezing (Brazis 2011, p. 89). The motor and reflex findings are usually more trustworthy than a numb patch.

**The two rules that do the work**

Morris gives the two rules every localizer of the limbs needs.

1. If a muscle is weak because of a nerve lesion, **every muscle that nerve supplies below the lesion must also be weak**. If brachioradialis is weak from a radial nerve lesion at the spiral groove, wrist and finger extension must be weak too; if they are not, the problem is elsewhere (Morris 2012, p. xxix).
2. To separate a root from a nerve, **test a muscle with the same root but a different nerve**. Quadriceps weakness could be the femoral nerve or the L2 to L4 roots; the hip adductors share those roots but travel in the obturator nerve, so they decide it (Morris 2012, p. 23).

**What changes in a child**

In children, root and nerve lesions are less often degenerative and more often traumatic, compressive or present from birth, and young children are poor reporters of numbness. That makes the motor exam and the reflexes, which do not depend on the child's description, even more important. The rest of this module applies the two rules, first to the arm, then to the leg, then to the newborn plexus.
keyPoints: Three maps overlap on every limb: dermatome, myotome and nerve territory.
Cutting a single dorsal root may cause little or no sensory loss, so normal sensation does not exclude a root lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 89).
Rule one: every muscle a nerve supplies below the lesion must be weak (Morris 2012, p. xxix).
Rule two: test a muscle with the same root but a different nerve (Morris 2012, p. 23).
In children, rely on motor findings and reflexes more than on reported numbness.

question.question: A 13-year-old has weak, wasted quadriceps and an absent knee reflex after a pelvic injury. Which single test best separates a femoral nerve lesion from a lesion of the L2 to L4 roots?
options: Strength of the hip adductors, which share the roots but travel in the obturator nerve
Strength of ankle dorsiflexion
Pinprick sensation over the front of the thigh
The ankle reflex
question.explanation: The hip adductors are supplied by the same L2 to L4 roots as the quadriceps but reach the muscle through the obturator nerve, so weak adductors point to the roots or plexus and strong adductors point to the femoral nerve (Morris 2012, p. 23). Ankle dorsiflexion depends mainly on L4 and L5 through the peroneal nerve, so it does not test the L2 to L3 roots. Sensation over the front of the thigh is shared by the femoral nerve and those roots, and root overlap makes it unreliable. The ankle reflex is S1 and does not speak to either candidate.

sections.title: The arm: choosing the muscle that discriminates
sections.content:
The figure above is a small machine for the two rules. Mark each muscle or reflex you tested as weak or normal, and it keeps only the roots, plexus trunks and nerves that explain everything you found. Each candidate that drops out tells you why. The muscle-to-root table inside it uses the **predominant** roots; sources differ by a segment here and there, so treat it as a teaching map, not a law.

**Wrist drop**

Try the preset. The wrist and fingers drop, and brachioradialis is weak, but triceps and its reflex are normal. The branches to triceps leave the radial nerve high in the arm, so sparing them puts the lesion at or below the spiral groove of the humerus, which is Morris's own example of rule one (Morris 2012, p. xxix). Now ask whether the C7 root could do it: no, because triceps depends mainly on C7 and is normal.

**Hand weakness: nerve or lower trunk?**

When the first dorsal interosseous is weak and wasted, ask about the thumb's short abductor. Both depend on the lowest cervical and first thoracic roots, but the interosseous travels in the ulnar nerve and the thumb abductor in the median nerve. A weak interosseous with a strong thumb abductor points to the **ulnar nerve**; both weak points higher, to the lower roots or the lower trunk of the plexus. This is rule two again, a shared root and a different nerve, and the figure computes it.

**What to test, in what order**

A practical sweep of the arm takes only a few muscles, chosen because they separate the candidates: shoulder abduction (axillary, mainly C5), elbow flexion (musculocutaneous, C5 and C6), elbow extension (radial, mainly C7), wrist and finger extension (radial), thumb abduction (median, mainly T1) and finger spreading (ulnar, mainly T1). Add the biceps, brachioradialis and triceps reflexes.

**In a child**

Turn strength testing into a contest, test one side at a time and compare the two. A child who will not cooperate with formal testing will often show you shoulder abduction, elbow extension and grip while reaching for a toy held high, to the side, or just out of reach.
keyPoints: A radial nerve lesion at the spiral groove spares triceps; the C7 root does not.
Weak first dorsal interosseous with a strong thumb abductor points to the ulnar nerve; both weak points to the lower roots or lower trunk.
Choose muscles that separate candidates rather than testing everything.
Root assignments vary by a segment between sources; the figure uses predominant roots.

question.question: A 15-year-old wakes with a wrist drop after sleeping with his arm over a chair back. Finger extensors and brachioradialis are weak; triceps and the triceps reflex are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: The C7 root
The posterior interosseous nerve in the forearm
The posterior cord of the brachial plexus
The radial nerve at or below the spiral groove of the humerus
question.explanation: Brachioradialis and the wrist and finger extensors are all radial nerve muscles, and triceps, whose branches leave the radial nerve high in the arm, is spared, which places the lesion at or below the spiral groove (Morris 2012, p. xxix). The C7 root is excluded because triceps depends mainly on C7 and is normal. The posterior interosseous nerve branches off after brachioradialis and the main wrist extensor are supplied, so it cannot weaken brachioradialis. A posterior cord lesion would also weaken deltoid and triceps.

sections.title: The leg: two kinds of foot drop
sections.content:
Foot drop is the commonest focal leg problem a neurologist is asked to localize, and it is a lovely test of method because two very different lesions produce it. The common peroneal nerve winds around the head of the fibula, just under the skin, where it is easily compressed. The L5 root supplies the same ankle dorsiflexors, and also muscles that the peroneal nerve never touches.

**The discriminating muscles**

Morris lays out the patterns. Weak dorsiflexion and eversion, with weak big-toe extension, and normal reflexes: a **common peroneal nerve** lesion; look for scars or bruising over the fibular head. Weak dorsiflexion, eversion **and inversion**, sometimes with weak hip abduction: an **L4/L5 root or plexus** lesion (Morris 2012, p. 26). Inversion is the key, because tibialis posterior is an L5 muscle carried by the tibial nerve. Hip abduction is the second check, because gluteus medius is an L5 muscle carried by the superior gluteal nerve. Neither belongs to the peroneal nerve.

Morris adds that weakness of big-toe extension may be the only motor sign of an L5 root lesion (Morris 2012, p. 29). When everything at the ankle is weak with a lost ankle reflex, think further: a neuropathy, a sciatic nerve lesion, or a root or plexus lesion affecting several segments (Morris 2012, p. 26).

**Testing inversion properly**

Inversion is easy to fake with hip rotation. Hold the shin still with one hand and move the foot into inversion with the other, then ask the child to hold it there (Morris 2012, p. 29).

**Using the figure**

Load the two foot-drop presets in the figure in the previous section and compare them. In the first, inversion and hip abduction are normal, and only the common peroneal nerve survives. In the second, they are weak, and only the L5 root survives, because three different nerves are involved and the root is the one thing they share.

**In a child**

Peroneal neuropathy in a child follows weight loss, a tight cast, prolonged squatting or kneeling, crossing the legs, or a knee injury. An L5 radiculopathy is unusual in a young child, so a convincing one deserves imaging to look for a cause.
keyPoints: Common peroneal lesion: weak dorsiflexion, eversion and big-toe extension; inversion and hip abduction normal (Morris 2012, p. 26).
L4/L5 root or plexus: inversion and often hip abduction are weak too (Morris 2012, p. 26).
Weak big-toe extension may be the only motor sign of an L5 root lesion (Morris 2012, p. 29).
Test inversion with the shin held still, so hip rotation cannot fake it.
A convincing L5 radiculopathy in a young child deserves imaging for a cause.

question.question: A 12-year-old who lost weight quickly has a foot drop. Dorsiflexion and eversion are weak; inversion and hip abduction are normal; the ankle reflex is normal. Where is the lesion?
options: The L5 root
The common peroneal nerve near the fibular head
The sciatic nerve
The tibial nerve
question.explanation: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with normal inversion and hip abduction is the common peroneal pattern (Morris 2012, p. 26); rapid weight loss removes the fat that cushions the nerve at the fibular head. The L5 root is excluded because tibialis posterior (inversion) and gluteus medius (hip abduction) are both L5 muscles, and both are normal. A sciatic lesion would weaken the tibial-nerve muscles as well, including inversion. A tibial nerve lesion weakens inversion and plantar flexion, not dorsiflexion and eversion.

sections.title: The brachial plexus at birth
sections.content:
A newborn whose arm lies still after a difficult delivery gives you the plexus problem in its purest form, with one extra difficulty: the patient cannot follow a single instruction. Everything has to be read from posture, spontaneous movement and reflexes.

**The two classic patterns**

Fisch's drawing starts with three horizontal trunks: C5 and C6 join to form the upper trunk at a spot called Erb's point, C7 forms the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 form the lower trunk (Fisch 2012, p. 30). Pearl and Emsellem describe the **upper trunk (C5, C6) lesion, Erb palsy**, usually associated with shoulder dystocia: weak shoulder abductors and external rotators, deltoid and biceps, with the arm hanging limply at the side, turned in and pronated (Pearl 2014, p. 80). They describe the **lower plexus injury, Klumpke palsy**, as weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles and finger flexors (Pearl 2014, p. 80). Note that Pearl groups C7 with the lower plexus here, whereas Fisch draws the lower trunk from C8 and T1 alone; the figure follows Fisch.

**Root or trunk? The branches that leave early**

Two nerves leave the roots before the plexus forms: the dorsal scapular nerve to the rhomboids, from C5, and the long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior, from the upper roots (Fisch 2012, p. 31). The suprascapular nerve leaves later, from the upper trunk itself (Fisch 2012, p. 35). This sequence is a ruler. If the rhomboids and serratus work but the deltoid, biceps and infraspinatus do not, the injury is beyond the roots, in the upper trunk. If the root-level muscles are weak too, the damage is at the roots, where the surgical questions are different.

**Examining the newborn arm**

Watch the infant's spontaneous movement and the Moro response, which shows whether each shoulder abducts and each elbow flexes ([[m02-the-exam|Module 2]] covers the Moro in detail). Feel the biceps reflex; in an upper trunk injury it is absent. Watch the hand: a grasp that works in an arm that otherwise hangs still says the lower trunk is intact. Look for winging of the scapula when the infant pushes against your hand, which tests serratus.

**Not every still arm is a plexus**

A clavicle or humerus fracture can make a newborn refuse to move a painful arm, and a perinatal stroke weakens the arm from above. The plexus is localized by a lower motor neuron pattern in a root distribution, with the reflex lost.
keyPoints: Upper trunk (C5, C6) birth injury, Erb palsy: arm hangs at the side, turned in and pronated; biceps reflex absent (Pearl 2014, p. 80).
Lower plexus injury, Klumpke palsy: weak intrinsic hand muscles and finger flexors (Pearl 2014, p. 80).
The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves leave the roots before the plexus; spared rhomboids and serratus place an injury beyond the roots (Fisch 2012, p. 31).
In a newborn, read the plexus from posture, the Moro response, the grasp and the biceps reflex.
A fracture or a perinatal stroke can also make a newborn's arm lie still.

question.question: A newborn's right arm hangs at the side, turned in and pronated. The biceps reflex is absent and the Moro response shows no right shoulder abduction or elbow flexion. The hand grasps well, and there is no winging of the scapula. Where is the injury?
options: The C5 and C6 roots, torn from the cord
The lower trunk of the brachial plexus
The upper trunk of the brachial plexus (Erb palsy)
The left cerebral hemisphere, from a perinatal stroke
question.explanation: Weak shoulder abduction and elbow flexion with an absent biceps reflex and a working hand is the upper trunk pattern (Pearl 2014, p. 80), and an intact serratus, whose nerve leaves the roots before the plexus, places the injury beyond the roots (Fisch 2012, p. 31). A root avulsion at C5 and C6 would weaken the root-level branches and could wing the scapula. The lower trunk carries the hand, which works here. A perinatal stroke produces an upper motor neuron pattern with reflexes kept, not an absent biceps reflex in a root distribution.

sections.title: Reflexes as root markers
sections.content:
A tendon reflex is a small, honest experiment. It does not depend on the child's effort, cooperation or description, and it tests one short loop: a stretch receptor, a sensory fibre, one or two cord segments, a motor neuron and a muscle. A lost reflex therefore localizes better than almost any sensory complaint.

**The segments**

Commonly used values, and the ones the figure in this module uses:

| Reflex | Main segments | Nerve |
|---|---|---|
| Biceps | C5, C6 | Musculocutaneous |
| Brachioradialis | C6 (with C5) | Radial |
| Triceps | C7 | Radial |
| Knee | L3, L4 | Femoral |
| Ankle | S1 | Tibial |

Sources differ by a segment. Brazis, for example, gives the knee as L2 to L4 and the ankle as S1 to S2 (Brazis 2011, p. 117). The order matters more than the exact boundaries.

**Lost here, brisk below: the cord's signature**

The same reflexes find the level of a spinal cord lesion. In a cord lesion, reflexes are lost at the level of the lesion and increased below it (Brazis 2011, p. 12; Morris 2012, p. xxix). An absent biceps reflex with a brisk triceps and brisk knee and ankle jerks puts the lesion in the cord at the C5 and C6 segments, a pattern [[m06-spinal-cord|Module 6]] develops.

**Getting a reflex in a child**

A reflex hammer looks like a weapon to a toddler, so it is used late, on the parent's lap, and turned into a toy ([[m02-the-exam|Module 2]]). If a reflex seems absent, reinforce it: ask the child to clench teeth or pull their hands apart while you tap. Compare sides every time. Asymmetry is often more informative than the absolute grade.

**What a lost reflex can and cannot tell you**

An absent ankle reflex on one side with weak plantar flexion and numbness on the outer foot points to S1. An absent ankle reflex on both sides, with stocking sensory loss, points instead to a length-dependent neuropathy ([[m04-motor-unit|Module 4]]). The reflex localizes the loop; the pattern of the other findings says which part of the loop is broken.
keyPoints: Reflex segments: biceps C5 and C6, brachioradialis mainly C6, triceps C7, knee L3 and L4, ankle S1; sources differ by a segment.
A reflex does not depend on effort or description, so it localizes more reliably than numbness.
In a cord lesion, reflexes are lost at the level and brisk below it (Brazis 2011, p. 12; Morris 2012, p. xxix).
Reinforce a reflex that seems absent, and always compare sides.
One-sided loss suggests a root or nerve; symmetric distal loss suggests a polyneuropathy.

question.question: A 16-year-old with back pain has an absent right ankle reflex, weak right plantar flexion and numbness of the outer right foot. Which additional finding would point to the S1 root rather than the tibial nerve?
options: Weak right ankle dorsiflexion
Weak right hip extension (gluteus maximus)
A brisk right knee reflex
Loss of vibration at both big toes
question.explanation: Gluteus maximus shares the S1 root but is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve, which leaves well above the tibial nerve, so weak hip extension points to the root rather than the tibial nerve (Morris 2012, p. 23 gives this same-root, different-nerve logic). Weak dorsiflexion belongs to the L4 and L5 roots through the peroneal nerve and would widen the lesion rather than separate these two. A brisk knee reflex does not help, since neither candidate involves L3 or L4. Bilateral loss of vibration at the toes suggests a length-dependent neuropathy, not a single S1 lesion.

quiz.question: A 14-year-old dislocated his shoulder. He cannot lift his arm out to the side and has a numb patch over the outer shoulder; elbow flexion and the biceps reflex are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: The C5 root
The upper trunk of the brachial plexus
The axillary nerve
The suprascapular nerve
quiz.explanation: Isolated weakness of shoulder abduction with numbness over the outer shoulder after a dislocation is an axillary nerve lesion, and the nerve's course around the humeral neck explains the injury. A C5 root lesion or an upper trunk lesion would also weaken biceps, which shares C5, and remove the biceps reflex; both are normal here, which is rule one of this module at work. The suprascapular nerve supplies the rotator cuff muscles on the shoulder blade and has no skin territory over the outer shoulder.

quiz.question: A 15-year-old has weak finger spreading, a wasted first dorsal interosseous and numbness of the little finger. Thumb abduction is strong. Where is the lesion?
options: The ulnar nerve
The lower trunk of the brachial plexus
The T1 root
The median nerve at the wrist
quiz.explanation: The first dorsal interosseous and the short thumb abductor share the lowest cervical and first thoracic roots but travel in different nerves, the ulnar and the median. A weak interosseous with a strong thumb abductor therefore points to the ulnar nerve, by the same-root, different-nerve rule. A lower trunk or T1 root lesion would weaken the thumb abductor too, because it depends mainly on T1. A median lesion at the wrist weakens the thumb abductor and spares the interosseous, the opposite pattern.

quiz.question: A 16-year-old has a foot drop. Dorsiflexion, eversion and inversion are weak, and so is hip abduction. The ankle reflex is normal. Where is the lesion?
options: The common peroneal nerve
The deep peroneal nerve
The tibial nerve
The L5 root
quiz.explanation: Weakness spreads across three nerves here: the peroneal (dorsiflexion and eversion), the tibial (inversion) and the superior gluteal (hip abduction). The one thing they share is the L5 root (Morris 2012, p. 26). The common peroneal nerve does not supply tibialis posterior or gluteus medius, so it cannot explain inversion or hip abduction weakness. The deep peroneal nerve explains even less, sparing eversion. A tibial lesion would not weaken dorsiflexion.

quiz.question: A newborn's arm hangs limp after a difficult delivery: no shoulder abduction, no elbow flexion, absent biceps reflex. This time the scapula wings when the infant pushes against your hand. What does the winging add?
options: Nothing, since winging is common in newborns
Serratus anterior is weak, so the injury involves the roots themselves, before the plexus forms
The lower trunk is also injured
The injury is in the spinal cord
quiz.explanation: The long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior leaves the upper roots before the plexus forms (Fisch 2012, p. 31), so a weak serratus moves the injury proximally, to the roots themselves, rather than the upper trunk. The lower trunk carries the hand muscles, which are not mentioned as weak, and winging does not test them. A cord lesion would not produce a root-distribution lower motor neuron pattern with an absent reflex in one arm. Winging is not a normal finding to be dismissed.

quiz.question: A 13-year-old describes electric pain shooting down the back of one leg when she coughs. Strength and reflexes are normal, and you find no sensory loss. What should you conclude about a root lesion?
options: A normal sensory exam does not exclude it, because neighbouring roots overlap on the skin
It is excluded, because a root lesion always numbs its dermatome
It is excluded, because the reflexes are normal
It is confirmed, because cough-provoked pain only comes from roots
quiz.explanation: Adjacent dorsal roots overlap so much that a single root lesion may cause little or no sensory loss, so a normal sensory exam does not rule a root lesion out (Brazis 2011, p. 89). Pain that shoots along a root's territory and worsens with coughing or straining is typical of root irritation (Brazis 2011, p. 89), but it suggests a root lesion rather than proving one, so 'confirmed' overreaches. Normal reflexes do not exclude it either; an irritative lesion can spare the reflex arc. 'Always numbs its dermatome' is exactly the misconception the overlap corrects.
